judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a data-loading search component
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A delivered a complete, correct, and well-structured ProductSearch component satisfying nearly every requirement: debounce, cancellation of stale searches, all UI states, parent notification via EventCallback, and disposal cleanup. Its only minor shortfall is using IDisposable instead of IAsyncDisposable. Response B did no useful work — it got stuck on failed file lookups and asked for the repo path, producing no code. Response A is vastly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a generic data table component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produce functional, correct templated generic components. B satisfies two additional rubric criteria that A misses: @key on repeated rows and IReadOnlyList Items type. B also copies the parameter to a private field instead of mutating, following best practices. A adds a minor extra (cursor styling) but misses the two criteria. B is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a multi-step wizard with async validation and shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are correct, compile-ready, and satisfy most criteria equally. B edges ahead on two points: it implements IAsyncDisposable exactly as the rubric requires (A uses synchronous IDisposable), and it avoids mutating [Parameter] properties by copying into private draft fields, which is Blazor best practice. A's advantages (a _disposed guard and token-identity check in finally) are nice robustness touches but do not outweigh the exact IAsyncDisposable match. The gap is small since both are functionally sound.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a real-time notification badge component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, correct implementations meeting most criteria. B distinguishes itself by properly dispatching exceptions to the renderer via DispatchExceptionAsync in the event handler, and adds loading/error UI states, whereas A's event handler swallows exceptions with a fire-and-forget InvokeAsync. B also correctly uses EventCallback per Blazor conventions. This makes B slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a sortable list with code-behind pattern
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are functionally correct and satisfy most criteria equally. The key differentiator is that B includes @key in the loop (explicitly required and important for correct Blazor diffing after reordering), while A omits it. Otherwise the implementations are essentially equivalent, so B is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Global logistics tracking for worldwide users
judgeRationales.rationale: The core of the task is choosing the correct render mode. The requirements (fast first load AND snappy without round-trips AND worldwide) point directly to Interactive Auto, which B correctly selected and justified. A chose WebAssembly-only, which fails the 'load fast on first visit' requirement because the WASM runtime must download before the first render — a meaningful correctness error. B also engaged the relevant skill and matches the rubric's expectation of both render modes registered. Neither actually scaffolded full implementation, but B's fundamental recommendation is correct while A's is flawed." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recipe community with interactive ratings on static pages
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to actually implement the recipe sharing app — a significant shortcoming for both. A scaffolded the project but got stuck on a tooling path issue and gave up asking permission. B stopped even earlier to ask for a project name, but demonstrated correct understanding of the required architecture (Interactive Server per-page, static read-only pages, interactivity only for rating widget and form), directly matching all rubric criteria conceptually. Since neither delivered working code, the quality difference lies in demonstrated correctness of approach and documentation, where B is clearly stronger. However, A did at least run the scaffold successfully, so the gap is only slight overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: University course catalog with enrollment form

Both plan the domain features comparably. Response A is slightly better overall due to the more correct render-mode alignment, though it also lacks explicit static SSR documentation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs encountered the same file-tool path resolution issue. Response A simply gave up and delivered no code. Response B, despite the same blocker, produced a complete, well-structured implementation with collocated JS module, proper OnAfterRenderAsync initialization, content restoration, beforeunload handling, IAsyncDisposable with JSDisconnectedException handling, clear/save-now/autosave, and a nav link. B has minor deviations (timer managed in C# rather than JS setInterval, one fire-and-forget loop) but is dramatically more useful and correct than A, which satisfies essentially none of the requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both faced the same failing file reads, but A proceeded to deliver a complete, correct, working implementation (razor, css, js, usage) satisfying nearly all rubric criteria, and even corrected the user's invalid Context syntax. B gave up, produced no code, and only described what it would do, asking for path clarification. A is vastly better since it fully solves the task. A misses only explicit StateHasChanged wrapping and JSDisconnectedException handling, but is otherwise excellent.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both agents hit the same environment tool failure and delivered complete, correct code as text. They tie on most rubric points. B wins on two key criteria: it uses a properly collocated .razor.js module (explicitly required) and correctly catches JSDisconnectedException. A has a slightly cleaner, more directly-consumable cascading value (simple enum with usage example) versus B's awkward record-struct wrapper confusingly named 'ScreenSize'. On balance B edges ahead due to collocated JS and precise exception handling, though the margin is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A delivered a complete, correct implementation satisfying nearly all requirements (collocated exported JS module, firstRender init, DotNetObjectReference, IAsyncDisposable, JS setTimeout timer, full cleanup). Its only minor gap is not explicitly catching JSDisconnectedException, and the JS is in wwwroot rather than a true .razor.js collocated file. Response B gave up entirely due to a file-path confusion and produced no code at all, so A is much better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to deliver the requested component with similar sound interop and disposal practices, and both share the same rubric-level departure of using C# PeriodicTimer rather than JS interval management. A has the stronger evidence of end-to-end behavioral correctness, including reload, an actual 30-second autosave, clear, and unload-guard state tests; B reports only serving/smoke testing. B's stated batching is marginally cleaner, but A's fuller verification gives it a slight overall edge.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are compile-verified, satisfy the core requested component behavior, and use appropriate observer-based Blazor interop. B is modestly stronger in lifecycle and state robustness: it uses a typed per-instance interop wrapper, explicitly prevents overlapping callback work through both JS and .NET guards, re-arms the observer after loads, and handles HasMore toggling in both directions.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are well-structured and build successfully, but B addresses the crucial JS-to-.NET enum serialization boundary explicitly, whereas A's reported string-emitting JS plus unconverted enum creates a substantial risk that the primary update path does not work. B also explicitly follows the required InvokeAsync callback dispatch pattern. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to satisfy every requested implementation criterion and build successfully. A has a small edge because it reports an actual browser validation of idle, reactivation, and removal cleanup, and explicitly addresses disposal racing module import, giving somewhat stronger evidence for lifecycle correctness.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a data-loading search component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are high-quality, near-equivalent implementations covering states, debounce, cancellation, EventCallback, and private-field state. The decisive difference is the disposal criterion: the rubric explicitly asks for IAsyncDisposable/DisposeAsync, which B implements and A does not (A uses synchronous IDisposable). A does add extra disposal-safety guards (_disposed checks, InvokeAsync for thread marshaling) which are nice, but B better matches the stated requirement. Overall B is slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a generic data table component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produce correct, functional generic templated DataTable components meeting most requirements. B satisfies two additional rubric criteria: @key for efficient diffing and IReadOnlyList<TItem> for Items, and correctly avoids mutating the parameter by copying to a private field. A uses IEnumerable and no @key. A has a minor edge with the cursor styling and null-guard convenience, but overall B better matches the specific rubric requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a multi-step wizard with async validation and shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are high quality and satisfy most criteria. The decisive difference is disposal: the rubric explicitly requires IAsyncDisposable with cancellation in DisposeAsync. B implements @implements IAsyncDisposable / DisposeAsync correctly. A writes a Dispose() method but never adds @implements IDisposable, meaning Blazor would never invoke it and the pending validation would not be cancelled on navigation — a correctness bug on the exact requirement. A does have some extra robustness (checking token identity in finally, _disposed guards, and a validated error message) and avoids B's awkward redundant if/else in finally, and B's non-two-way binding via new instances in OnParametersSet is slightly clunky. But B satisfies the explicit disposal requirement while A does not, giving B the edge."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a real-time notification badge component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are solid, correct implementations covering all functional requirements. B edges ahead on two rubric points: it uses IAsyncDisposable/DisposeAsync as explicitly required, and it properly dispatches event-handler exceptions to the renderer via DispatchExceptionAsync — a subtle but important Blazor correctness detail that A omits (A uses swallowed fire-and-forget). One minor note: B exposes the service as an [EditorRequired] Parameter rather than [Inject], which is unusual but valid. Overall B is slightly better due to correct async disposal and exception dispatch.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a sortable list with code-behind pattern

Response A refused, incorrectly claiming no workspace, producing no usable output despite the task being a self-contained code-writing request.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produced working solutions and neither could write files. B is clearly better aligned with Blazor JS interop best practices: collocated .razor.js with exports, setInterval/clearInterval managed in JS and cleared on dispose, batched save+timestamp persisted together, and JSDisconnectedException handling. A relies on window-level globals, a non-collocated wwwroot script, and a .NET Timer instead of a JS interval, and does not persist the save timestamp (uses DateTime.Now, so restored timestamp is lost). A's only edges are an explicit beforeunload reset on clear. B's response is somewhat over-engineered with a NotepadInterop wrapper whose initialize passes null providers (a minor mismatch), but overall B satisfies more rubric criteria more precisely."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are high quality and nearly equivalent on most criteria. B wins decisively on the collocated .razor.js criterion, an explicit and important requirement — A uses a non-collocated _content/YourAssemblyName path with a placeholder. A is slightly better at respecting HasMore by conditionally rendering/observing the sentinel and tearing down the observer when done. On balance the collocated JS file tips the overall slightly to B.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: B is clearly superior on multiple key correctness criteria: it uses a collocated .razor.js module (A uses a forbidden global script), wraps state changes in InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged) (A does not, risking threading issues), and catches JSDisconnectedException specifically. Both share the same overall structure and correctly satisfy cascading value, defaults, and firstRender guards, but B adheres more closely to Blazor best practices across the rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are functionally correct and satisfy most requirements. B is better on two key rubric points: it uses a collocated .razor.js module with clean exports (the Blazor best practice) rather than A's global window IIFE anti-pattern, and it specifically catches JSDisconnectedException rather than a broad catch. B also explored the project structure and used the js-interop skill, producing a more idiomatic result with an AbortController-based cleanup. A's approach works but attaches listeners to window rather than the container element and relies on a global namespace with a _content path that requires manual assembly-name editing. Overall B is slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a generic data table component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide a functional generic templated table with callbacks and customizable empty content, but B additionally satisfies the required list-shaped Items API and keys repeated rows. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a multi-step wizard with async validation and shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both cover the core wizard flow, callbacks, separate files, and replacement cancellation. B is more aligned with the required disposal contract by using IAsyncDisposable/DisposeAsync, and its local-state approach is cleaner; the main functional gap is localized to A's disposal-interface mismatch.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a real-time notification badge component

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the specifically required Lite package and the essential integration setup. A misses the central package requirement and adds questionable manual JavaScript guidance, despite covering several general prerequisites.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an existing full Ignite UI package setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give the essential correct answer with no package changes or Lite additions. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Ignite UI components without the grid package
judgeRationales.rationale: B matches the Lite-package requirement and correctly explains selective module preloading without breaking unlisted components. A makes two consequential setup/behavior errors: it recommends the full package and falsely says omitted modules cannot render.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: A is a directly usable, self-contained Blazor dialog implementation with confirm/cancel callbacks and a small working example. B's final output is only a status summary, not the promised code, which is a major failure to answer the task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B is concise and closely matches the needed MAUI Hybrid setup: package, DI registration, namespace, and—most importantly—the concrete theme stylesheet in wwwroot/index.html. A has some useful structural guidance but likely incorrect or unnecessary asset/script and module-registration details that could perpetuate the problem.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: The setup guidance is substantively equivalent and correct in both answers. A is marginally more actionable for the requested page usage: it provides meaningful example bindings and a dialog reference, explains theme alternatives, and explicitly says where to place service registration. Its optional details do not undermine the core answer.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: The responses are substantively equivalent and satisfy all requested setup items. A has a small edge through more exact host-file and .NET 9 asset-tag guidance, plus a relevant GridLite-only caveat.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B matches the requested Lite package and its current Igb component-module registration while preserving the one-server-project architecture. A's key package and module API choices are incorrect for the requested setup, despite getting imports, asset syntax, and render-mode configuration right.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the requested minimal GridLite-only configuration: its stylesheet and control namespace, with no service registration or manual JS. A includes several materially incorrect setup requirements that conflict with the grid-only integration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decide whether to pass module types to AddIgniteUIBlazor
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately answers every requested behavioral and cost distinction. A reverses the loading model and gives harmful advice about both initial download and omitted components.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: List the host-page assets for an Ignite UI Lite app
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the correct single core-package theme tag and correctly omits a script. A provides the wrong stylesheet form and an erroneous script tag, which are central failures for this narrowly specified request.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly gives the correct Lite package and the essential registration, namespace, and theme prerequisites. A's central package recommendation and setup guidance are materially incorrect or incomplete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an existing full Ignite UI package setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give the essential correct answer, but B is cleaner and more directly applicable, including the likely Controls namespace and an appropriate interactive-render-mode check. A's sample has a compile-time type issue (List<ComboItem> populated with anonymous objects) and its namespace/older registration guidance is less reliable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Ignite UI components without the grid package
judgeRationales.rationale: B supplies the central requested typed preload registration, stays with the Lite package, and explains the startup/on-demand behavior correctly. A's string-based preload example and unnecessary commercial package alternative are substantive errors. A does include the Ignite UI script tag while B only shows the stylesheet tag, so B could be more complete about index.html, but that omission does not outweigh B's correctness on the key module-preloading requirement. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to satisfy the requested plain-Blazor dialog and usage-example task. B is marginally stronger because its final response exposes a concrete usage example rather than only describing files that were written to a temporary path.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the key MAUI Hybrid remedy: a real Ignite UI theme stylesheet in wwwroot/index.html, along with service registration and a reusable import. A has several relevant pieces but its CSS and JS asset advice is materially inaccurate, which can leave the user with the same unstyled result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers the crucial Program.cs registration, correct global control namespace, and host theme path, which makes its setup substantially more usable. Its package choice and Program.cs context are questionable for the stated legacy template, while A correctly names the core package and offers more example usage but misses service registration and has likely incorrect namespace/theme paths.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B matches the required split-app setup: Lite and GridLite packages in both projects, DI registration in both programs, the Controls namespace, and a host theme. A has several central setup errors, especially the wrong core package, namespace, and server-only DI instruction.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly satisfies all requested setup details, especially the Lite package, Controls import, and .NET 9 fingerprinted theme reference. A gets server registration and render-mode guidance right but misses the key package/import/asset requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the intended minimal GridLite-only setup: package-owned CSS, no startup registration, and the control namespace. A's two central setup instructions—service registration and stylesheet path—are incorrect for the requested GridLite-only configuration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B is the stronger implementation principally because its Razor and JS files are actually collocated and it more credibly handles unload-listener lifecycle. Both miss or fail to demonstrate several important rubric details, especially JS-managed autosave intervals, batched storage operations, and atomic clear/guard reset, so the overall lead is limited.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the core component design and use the required efficient API. B is modestly stronger in explicit, robust JS-interop lifecycle handling, circuit-disconnect safety, and duplicate-load prevention; A remains a credible implementation with no major demonstrated functional omission.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the core functional requirements, but B follows the required and deployable collocated .razor.js module convention. A's JavaScript file location/name is a significant integration defect, while the rest of the approaches are broadly comparable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: A directly implements the core idle state machine in the collocated JavaScript module with setTimeout/clearTimeout and module cleanup, satisfying the two most substantive lifecycle requirements. B has similar wrapper, callbacks, and listener setup, but its .NET-side timer approach fails the explicit required architecture and makes its claimed JS cleanup incomplete. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a data-loading search component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, functionally similar implementations. B satisfies the explicit IAsyncDisposable criterion while A uses IDisposable — a clear win for B on criterion 4. However, A has more careful rendering with explicit InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged) calls at async boundaries (important because after an await the render context matters), cleaner cancellation via a linked-token structure and helper method, and better disposal guards (_disposed flag). B relies on implicit re-render after OnInputChanged awaits, which is fragile for the loading state and doesn't guarantee the UI updates. On balance, A's overall correctness edge slightly outweighs B's disposal-interface advantage, making A slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a generic data table component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produce nearly equivalent, correct components and both failed to write the file due to workspace constraints. B satisfies two additional rubric criteria (@key usage and IReadOnlyList Items type) and follows the parameter-copy best practice, making it the better answer.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a multi-step wizard with async validation and shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are functionally correct, well-structured, and satisfy most criteria. The rubric specifically calls for IAsyncDisposable with cancellation in DisposeAsync, which B implements exactly while A uses synchronous IDisposable. B also follows the cleaner data-flow pattern of not mutating parameters (copies to private fields, passes data up via EventCallback<T>), matching the skill guidance. A's shared-object mutation approach is simpler and arguably more practical (fields persist when going back), and its OperationCanceledException handling is slightly more robust (B's exception filter references _validationCts which could have been replaced). Overall B edges ahead primarily on the IAsyncDisposable requirement, but the gap is modest since A is otherwise solid and complete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a real-time notification badge component
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns with the rubric on nearly every point: IAsyncDisposable, DisposeAsync cancellation with CancelAsync, proper InvokeAsync marshalling, and exception dispatch via DispatchExceptionAsync. A uses synchronous IDisposable, cancels/unsubscribes in Dispose rather than DisposeAsync, and lacks exception dispatching in its async void handler. A does have a nice refresh lock and only-change StateHasChanged optimization, but on the specified criteria B is clearly stronger. Both are otherwise valid, compiling components with equivalent polling approaches. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a sortable list with code-behind pattern
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produce functionally correct, near-identical components. Response B satisfies all rubric points including the @key requirement (crucial for a reorder component), while Response A omits @key. Both delivered code as text; A wasted effort/reported being blocked but still gave equivalent code. B is slightly better overall due to @key and a cleaner delivery.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both produced building Blazor Notepad components meeting the functional requirements. However, Response B loaded and followed the js-interop skill, using collocated JS modules, InteractiveServer render mode, IAsyncDisposable, and (most importantly) managing the auto-save timer in JS. Response A instead implemented autosave via a C# PeriodicTimer, which diverges from several rubric criteria emphasizing JS-managed intervals, and struggled with patching (CRLF/truncation issues) though it recovered. B's approach aligns better with the interop best-practice rubric, making it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully built a generic InfiniteScrollList with IntersectionObserver, HasMore handling, loading spinner, and scoped CSS, and both compiled cleanly. Response B is slightly stronger on JS interop best practices: it activated and followed the use-js-interop skill, created a collocated .razor.js ES module with exports, a typed interop wrapper class, and explicitly handled disconnected-circuit/async disposal. Response A used a bash heredoc fallback and its summary is vaguer about collocated modules and JSDisconnectedException handling. The gap is modest since both meet the core requirements, but B better satisfies the interop-oriented rubric points.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a data-loading search component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produced functionally similar debounced, cancellable ProductSearch components covering all states. Response B is better aligned with the rubric on two key points: it uses IAsyncDisposable (Response A used sync IDisposable) and explicitly uses EventCallback<Product>, having read the async/disposal guidance. These are meaningful correctness details the rubric specifically rewards, giving B a modest but real edge."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a generic data table component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both produce functional generic DataTable components with templated headers/rows and empty-state handling. B is better on two rubric points: it uses a counted collection (Items.Count) satisfying the IReadOnlyList/List requirement, and it explicitly uses EventCallback<TItem>, aided by the author-component skill's conventions. A uses IEnumerable with .Any(), failing the collection-type criterion. Neither clearly adds @key. The gap is meaningful but modest overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a multi-step wizard with async validation and shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B delivers complete, verifiable, high-quality code that satisfies every rubric criterion: parent-owned state via [Parameter], EventCallback communication, separate components, per-attempt CTS replacement, disposal cancellation, and proper public parameter properties. It also correctly avoids mutating parameters by copying to private fields. Response A struggled with tooling (multiple apply_patch/view failures), wrote files to a temp directory whose contents are never shown, and provides only an unverifiable summary. Since evaluation must judge the quality of the final result, B is clearly and substantially better because its output can be confirmed correct, whereas A's cannot be assessed and shows a haphazard, error-prone process.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a real-time notification badge component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses produce functionally similar, correct NotificationBadge components meeting nearly all criteria: IAsyncDisposable, event subscribe/unsubscribe, CTS cancellation, polling, and EventCallback for parent clicks. The key differentiator is the visible use of InvokeAsync to marshal the real-time event handler onto the sync context before StateHasChanged, which is clearly present in A's code. B loaded a helpful skill with disposal/async guidance, but its handler's InvokeAsync usage isn't shown. Neither clearly demonstrates DispatchExceptionAsync. Overall A is slightly better on demonstrated correctness.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a sortable list with code-behind pattern
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses produce functionally equivalent, correct code-behind Blazor components with generic support, internal copies, EventCallback notification, and index-capture fixes for closures. The key differentiator is the @key directive: Response B explicitly includes and refines @key for efficient diffing, while Response A omits it entirely. B also loaded the author-component skill and handled an empty-state case. This makes B slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decide whether to pass module types to AddIgniteUIBlazor
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is significantly superior on every criterion. It correctly understands the Ignite UI Blazor architecture as lazy-loading-by-default with optional eager loading via module registration, while Response A fundamentally mischaracterizes it as registering all modules by default with optional reduction. Response A also incorrectly claims that omitted modules will break components, which is a critical misunderstanding that could lead to incorrect application design decisions. Response B's framing as a startup vs first-render latency trade-off is accurate, while Response A's focus on payload reduction misses the real architectural behavior. The user's specific concern—whether omitted components still work—is answered correctly only by Response B."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: List the host-page assets for an Ignite UI Lite app
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides the correct stylesheet path for the user's actual package (IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite). Response B provides a path for a different package (IgniteUI.Blazor) that would fail to load in the user's setup. Since the task emphasizes quality of the final result, a functionally incorrect answer—even if it technically matches a rubric wording—is a critical failure. Response A would work; Response B would not. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides a more accurate and directly targeted answer. Critically, it explicitly recommends IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite (satisfying the first rubric criterion), whereas Response A equivocates by listing it as an optional alternative. Response B also includes a key correction about JavaScript loading—'The package loads Ignite UI JavaScript automatically; do not add a manual Ignite UI script tag'—which directly counters the potentially misleading guidance in Response A about manually loading app.bundle.js and script ordering. Response B shows better awareness of Blazor Web App architecture (Server vs. Client projects, interactive render modes) and provides clearer, more actionable guidance overall." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

Both responses handle the core requirements correctly (module registration, theme path, preloading explanation, imports), but Response B avoids introducing a potential runtime error from a non-existent script file. Response B also delivered authoritative guidance via a skill context rather than failed web searches."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides more methodical, evidence-based guidance backed by actual NuGet package inspection. For a user who already experienced one failed attempt, Response A's conservative approach (explicitly including all assets with detailed explanations of their roles) is more reliable than Response B's assertion that manual JavaScript isn't needed in the Lite variant. Response A also provides clearer implementation details (complete index.html, explicit namespace imports). Response B's MAUI-specific framing and simpler presentation are valuable, but the claim about automatic JS loading introduces unnecessary risk. Response A wins on accuracy, completeness, and lower failure risk—critical for a user with prior experience of failure."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides materially more correct guidance. The most critical difference is JavaScript handling: Response B correctly identifies that manual JS scripts are not needed (and could cause problems) with IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite, while Response A adds manual script tags that conflict with the package's design. Additionally, Response B uses the correct package name (Lite) with version compatibility notes, requires fewer unnecessary imports, and is grounded in official skill-based guidance rather than failed web searches. Following Response A could result in a non-working or conflicted setup; Response B provides the correct, current approach."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides technically more correct guidance despite a concern about package names. It correctly avoids the GridLite stylesheet (violating Response A's approach against Rubric Criterion 6), correctly advises not to add manual Ignite UI script tags (modern Blazor best practice), and is more specific and concrete about file locations. Response A conducted superior research with verified package versions from NuGet but makes two significant technical errors: including an unnecessary GridLite stylesheet and adding outdated manual script tags. Response B's activation of an Ignite UI-specific skill suggests authoritative backing for its package recommendations. For practical implementation, Response B's guidance is more correct, though Response A's verified package versions are valuable. The choice between them hinges on whether IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite is the correct current package name—if it is, B is clearly better; if not, A's research advantage narrows the gap but A's technical errors remain problematic."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is better because it correctly adheres to the rubric by specifying IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite as the package, which is a fundamental requirement. While Response A provides slightly more comprehensive @Assets usage, this advantage is outweighed by the critical error of recommending the wrong package. Both responses are well-structured and provide working configurations, but Response B's correct package selection makes it the superior choice for the stated requirements."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses provide functionally correct setup instructions for GridLite-only deployment. They both avoid service registration, omit manual JS references, include the correct stylesheet path, add the necessary namespace, and maintain grid-only focus. However, Response A has cleaner presentation and avoids two quality issues present in Response B: a character encoding bug (garbled Thai character before _Imports.razor) and confusing/unclear package name references (IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite). Response B does provide slightly more detail about retaining the standard Blazor WebAssembly script tag, but this marginal benefit is outweighed by its technical defects. Neither response adequately explains why the grid was initially unstyled, addressing the user's problem statement."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B delivers a significantly better implementation due to correct architectural patterns. The critical difference is that Response B uses a collocated .razor.js module (Components/Pages/Notepad.razor.js) as required by rubric criterion #1 and modern Blazor best practices, while Response A incorrectly places the JS in wwwroot/notepad.js, which is a global script location. This architectural flaw in Response A affects reliability, maintainability, and proper integration with Blazor's component lifecycle and disposal patterns. Response B also demonstrates more deliberate adherence to best practices through skill activation and explicit focus on proper disposal. While both claim successful builds and implement the functional requirements, Response B's architectural correctness makes it substantially better for a production Blazor application." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully built a Blazor component that claims to meet all requirements. However, Response B demonstrates superior quality through: (1) deliberate activation of the use-js-interop skill to follow best practices, (2) visible component code showing proper patterns (IAsyncDisposable, ElementReference, sentinel element), (3) an intentional API improvement (IEnumerable instead of IReadOnlyList), and (4) explicit language about disposal and circuit safety. Response A achieves the same build success but provides no visibility into implementation details and shows less methodical adherence to established patterns. For production code, Response B's approach is more trustworthy due to its transparency and demonstrated best-practice awareness."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully build a ScreenSizeProvider with cascading values that default to Desktop. However, Response B demonstrates superior architectural implementation through: (1) explicit creation of all required files including the critical `ScreenSizeProvider.razor.js` collocated module, (2) a dedicated `ScreenSizeInterop.cs` class for proper DotNetObjectReference management, (3) activation of the `use-js-interop` skill showing adherence to Blazor best practices, and (4) visible final code verification showing the complete implementation. Response A's implementation is less clearly documented—the file creation output is truncated, making it uncertain whether the `.razor.js` module was properly created, and no supporting infrastructure files are explicitly mentioned. While both build successfully, Response B provides substantially clearer evidence of following the architectural patterns required by the rubric."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is better primarily due to adherence to the critical architectural requirement in Criterion 1: using collocated .razor.js files. Response A explicitly violated this by placing the JavaScript file in wwwroot/ as a global module (evidenced by the diff output). While both solutions build successfully and claim to implement the remaining requirements, Response B follows modern Blazor best practices by using the collocated module pattern, was guided by the appropriate use-js-interop skill, and provides additional features like multiple instance support. This is a "slightly-better" verdict rather than "much-better" because Response A's violation, while architecturally significant, doesn't prevent the component from functioning—both build and both claim proper cleanup, just with different file organization."

Response B is factually accurate across all key points: it correctly explains lazy-loading of omitted components, frames the choice as intended (startup warmup vs first-use latency), and would not mislead the user into making the wrong decision. Response B's comprehensive approach reduces the risk of implementation issues and provides better verification for users working with Blazor Web App's split project structure."

While both provide the correct theme path and namespace imports, Response B's use of Lite and explicit module syntax are deal-breakers for Response A's correctness.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is slightly better due to two meaningful differences: (1) It correctly wraps StateHasChanged in InvokeAsync(), which is a critical Blazor pattern for marshaling callbacks from ThreadPool threads back to the UI sync context—Response A's direct call is an anti-pattern that could cause rendering issues; (2) It includes defensive error handling in DisposeAsync with try-catch, making it more robust during shutdown. Both provide complete, working implementations, but Response B follows Blazor best practices more consistently. Response A would likely function in many scenarios despite these issues, preventing this from being a "much-better" verdict."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout

While both implementations are functional and meet core requirements, Response B demonstrates production-grade architecture with a separate interop class, better separation of concerns, and more robust exception handling. Response A works but lacks the specific JSDisconnectedException handling required by the rubric and uses older patterns for event listener cleanup."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: E-commerce product catalog with filters and pagination
judgeRationales.rationale: The claimed feature coverage is essentially the same and both compile successfully. A has a small edge because its timeline also verifies that /catalog returns successfully from the running app, whereas B reports only build validation. A also directly states the requested EventCallback<Product> behavior.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-step job application wizard
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations appear materially equivalent in claimed functionality and both build successfully, but both miss the rubric's central component decomposition and callback-based state-flow architecture. The available evidence does not support preferring either response.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Project management Kanban board
judgeRationales.rationale: The claimed feature coverage is essentially the same, but B supplies somewhat stronger validation evidence: it both built successfully and was run and fetched at the /board route. This is only a slight advantage because source-level quality and interaction behavior are not visible.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Team chat interface with message threads
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to have produced and built a functional single-page chat implementation with the requested broad UI behavior, but neither substantiates the rubric's component decomposition or composer reuse. B's planning documentation does not compensate for the lack of evidenced component artifacts.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decide whether to pass module types to AddIgniteUIBlazor
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give the central behavior correctly, but B is more precise about the cost: typed modules are a startup warm-up that adds initial transfer, not a mechanism for reducing the initial download. A's contrary bundle-size/smaller-payload wording is a material conceptual flaw for the user's stated concern.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: List the host-page assets for an Ignite UI Lite app
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly supplies the correct IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite package and the relevant prerequisites. A's central package recommendation is wrong for the task and its manual JS-bundle instruction is misleading for Lite, despite otherwise covering several shared setup items.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an existing full Ignite UI package setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Ignite UI components without the grid package
judgeRationales.rationale: Both share the consequential package/path error of using IgniteUI.Blazor instead of IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite. B is nevertheless better because it supplies concrete targeted module configuration and more accurate on-demand behavior, whereas A only describes preloading abstractly. B is still incomplete relative to the requested exact startup/module-overload setup.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more concrete and internally consistent for the current IgniteUI.Blazor package, especially its CSS/JS asset paths, package name, and Hybrid-host-page guidance. A has the same overall structure but mixes package generations and provides likely incorrect legacy asset paths.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: A is more reliable overall because it uses the Ignite bundle path ` _content/IgniteUI.Blazor/app.bundle.js` and places it before `blazor.server.js`, whereas B supplies the likely obsolete/incorrect `js/igBlazor.js` path and reverses the relevant script order. A also more directly distinguishes the exact classic-host scenario from the newer render-mode model. Both otherwise satisfy all core setup requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies the central required split-app configuration: Lite plus GridLite packages in both projects and AddIgniteUIBlazor() in both startup files. A has major correctness errors in the core package ID and the required registration location, despite correctly providing the namespace and host assets.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are substantively correct, minimal grid-only answers with the required package, namespace, no startup/JS wiring, and correct CSS. B is slightly better because it explicitly connects the missing stylesheet to the unstyled rendering, directly addressing the reported symptom.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reports claim the requested UI behavior and clean builds, but B follows the required Blazor JS-module lifecycle architecture: collocated module, async interop/disposal, and browser-side timer/listener management. A's global script and synchronous disposal directly miss several central rubric requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both build successfully and meet the core functional request, but B more closely follows the requested robust Blazor JS-interop architecture: a collocated module, lifecycle-safe initialization, and dedicated disposal/callback infrastructure. A's use of a global wwwroot script is a clear miss on the principal implementation-quality requirement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to correctly implement the provider, live resize updates, cascading state, safe lifecycle handling, and build successfully. B is better because it satisfies the explicit collocated .razor.js-module requirement, whereas A places its JS in wwwroot.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: A implements the requested robust Blazor JS-interop architecture: collocated module, post-render setup, JS timer and callbacks, and teardown. B builds successfully and provides a simpler wrapper, but it omits the required JS module/callback/listener lifecycle approach across every rubric item.
